client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away two months ago. Every time there's a family get-together, I just feel this wave of sadness that I can't shake, and it kind of ruins everything for me. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because she's still gone no matter what I say here.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — grief can feel especially heavy when it keeps surfacing in moments that used to feel joyful, like family gatherings. I notice that even as you're sharing something so painful, there's a kind of quiet exhaustion in how you're expressing it, almost like the weight of it has been sitting with you for a long time in silence. I wonder — when you say talking won't change anything, is part of you feeling not just sad, but maybe a little worn down or hopeless about finding any relief at all?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I think that's pretty accurate, actually. It's not just sadness — it's more like I've been carrying this thing around for so long that I've kind of stopped expecting it to get better. And honestly, part of me wonders if talking about it just... reopens something I've worked hard to keep closed, you know?
therapist: That image of keeping something carefully closed makes a lot of sense — it can feel like protection, especially when you've been managing this largely on your own. And yet, I'm noticing something gentle but a little tentative in the way you're describing all of this, like part of you is still quietly testing whether it might be safe to set that weight down, even just a little. What do you think it would feel like to let yourself explore this, even knowing it might sting — do you think there's a difference between *reopening* a wound and actually beginning to tend to it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think I understand what you're getting at, but honestly, in the moment it doesn't really feel that different to me. Like, whether I call it reopening or tending, it still hurts, and I'm not sure I trust that the hurting is actually going to lead somewhere better. I've sat with this loneliness for so long that it's almost become familiar, and the idea of poking at it feels more risky than just... leaving it alone.
therapist: What you're describing — that loneliness becoming almost like a familiar companion — is something a lot of people experience, and it makes complete sense that the known, even when painful, can feel safer than the uncertain. I'm curious though, as you were talking just now, there seemed to be something a little more alive in your voice than your words might suggest — almost like a part of you is more engaged with this than you're quite ready to admit. What do you think that part might be saying, if it felt safe enough to speak up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess... maybe there is a part of me that's tired of it, you know? Like tired of coming home to silence every night and convincing myself that's fine, that I prefer it that way. But admitting that feels dangerous somehow, like if I actually let myself want connection, I'm just setting myself up to be disappointed again.
therapist: That moment of honesty — admitting you're tired of the silence — took real courage, and it sounds like underneath the grief there's also a deep longing for connection that you've been quietly talking yourself out of. The fear that wanting something means risking loss again makes so much sense, especially when loss is still so fresh and present for you. I'm wondering, when you imagine actually letting yourself want that connection, what's the specific fear — is it that people will leave, or more that you'll somehow be too much, or not enough?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, it's more that I'll be too much. Like, if I actually let people see how lonely I've been, or how much I'm still carrying from losing my dad, they'll get tired of it and pull away. And then I'd be worse off than I am now, because at least right now the silence is something I'm used to.
therapist: The fear of being "too much" is such a painful place to live — it means you've been quietly editing yourself, carrying your grief about both your grandmother *and* your dad largely alone, to protect others from a weight that was never yours to hide in the first place. There's something that strikes me about the way you said that — softly, almost carefully — like even here, you're being mindful not to take up too much space. I'm curious, where do you think you first learned that your grief or your needs might be too much for someone to stay for?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think... it was probably my dad, the way he'd shut down or leave the room whenever things got too emotional, like feelings were this inconvenient thing he didn't have the bandwidth for. So I just learned pretty early that if I wanted him to stay, I had to be smaller, quieter, easier to be around.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — you learned to make yourself smaller not because you *were* too much, but because the person who should have been able to hold your feelings simply couldn't, and a young child will almost always decide that's their fault rather than the adult's limitation. I noticed something shift as you said that — there was a kind of quickness to it, like the words were coming faster than maybe you expected, as if this realization has some real energy behind it. I'm wondering, sitting with that right now, what does it feel like to see that the "too much" story was something you were handed, rather than something that was ever actually true about you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: It feels... strange, honestly, like part of me wants to believe what you're saying, but there's this other part that immediately pushes back and goes "but what if it really was you, though." I think I've been carrying this story for so long that it almost feels like if I let go of it, I don't know who I am without it. It's weird to think that something so central to how I see myself might have just been someone else's limitation handed to me like it was a fact.
therapist: What you just said — that letting go of the story feels like losing a piece of yourself — is one of the most honest and important things a person can recognize in this kind of work, and it makes complete sense that it would feel disorienting. That "but what if it really was you" voice has been protecting you in its own way for a very long time, so of course it doesn't give up easily. I'm curious — if that story *wasn't* true, if you really weren't too much, what might become possible for you that feels impossible right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I sit with that question for a moment, and honestly my first instinct is to kind of deflect or laugh it off, because it feels almost too big to answer. Like, if I wasn't too much, maybe I could actually let people get close without constantly waiting for them to pull away or get tired of me. But even saying that out loud feels dangerous, like I'm setting myself up for something.
therapist: The fact that you said it out loud anyway, even while it felt dangerous, tells me something important — there's a part of you that's ready to want more than the silence, even if another part is bracing for impact. I notice there was something almost urgent in the way you said it, like the words were pushing to get out faster than you could second-guess them, which makes me wonder if this longing for closeness is bigger and more alive in you than you've been allowing yourself to acknowledge. What would it mean to just let that want exist for a moment, without immediately attaching the fear of what could go wrong?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, it did feel urgent, like I couldn't hold it back anymore, and that actually kind of scares me because I'm not used to wanting things that much. If I let myself really sit with that want, it feels almost too big, like if I acknowledge how lonely I actually am, I won't be able to stuff it back down again. And I guess part of me is wondering, what's the point of wanting closeness if every time I've reached for it, something goes wrong?
therapist: The fear that acknowledging the loneliness means you won't be able to contain it again — that's such a real and understandable fear, but I also notice that even as you're describing something that feels overwhelming, there's a kind of quiet steadiness underneath it, like you're actually holding this better than you're giving yourself credit for. And that question — "what's the point of wanting closeness if it keeps going wrong" — I don't think that's hopelessness talking as much as it's exhaustion from a pattern that was never really about your worth to begin with. I'm wondering, when you think about the times connection *has* gone wrong, do you think it was because you wanted too much, or because you were reaching toward people who, like your dad, simply didn't have the capacity to meet you there?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me, because my instinct is to say "no, it was me, I asked for too much" — but when I actually think about specific people, like my dad, like my ex, there's this pattern where they were just... not available in the way I needed. I guess I've been carrying this assumption that wanting closeness is inherently a burden I'm placing on people, but maybe that's not the same as actually being too much. It's just really hard to separate those two things when the outcome always felt the same — me ending up alone.
therapist: What you just did — actually examining the evidence and separating "I wanted too much" from "they weren't available" — is a genuinely significant shift, and I want to reflect that back to you because it matters. And yet, even as you're arriving at something that sounds like a real insight, there's something in your voice that sounds quieter, almost smaller, like the weight of all those endings is still sitting very heavily right now. I'm wondering if part of what makes it hard to fully take in this new way of seeing things is that the loneliness at the end of each story felt the same, regardless of whose limitation it was — and that pain is real, even if the meaning you've attached to it needs rewriting.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
